newsitem.title: USA: Market reaction concern in Fed price stability bid.
newsitem.headline: Market reaction concern in Fed price stability bid.

text.p: As the Federal Reserve strives to win the latest round of its inflation battle, it is highly sensitive to the impact of policy on temperamental financial markets, sources at the central bank told Reuters.

While the Fed sets two short-term interest rates -- the federal funds rate and the discount rate -- it has no control over long-term rates which are set by the market and based on inflation expectations and an array of perceived risks.
It is these bond rates which serve as a benchmark for consumer loans such as mortgages and which consequently play a key role in the economic growth formula.
"What matters is long-term rates," one senior Fed official told Reuters, referring to the broad impact of higher long-term yields on the economy.

Another Fed source said that while the Fed's 1994 preemptive tightening cycle succeeded in stabilizing inflation, the central bank found it difficult to convince the market the rapid-fire rate hikes were preventive in nature, and not a sign the Fed was behind the inflation curve.

As a result of market uncertainty, the 30-year Treasury bond yield soared from 6.0 percent in early 1994 to over 8.0 percent in November. It was not until the Fed raised the funds and the discount rates by 75 points each on November 15, 1994, that the bond market became convinced the Fed was indeed ahead of the inflation curve.
"In part, it's a communication problem," a second Fed source said.

The 75-basis-point move on the discount rate was the largest change in the symbolic rate since the Fed lowered the discount rate by 100 basis points in December 1991, at the urging of then Fed vice-chairman David Mullins, sources said.
The 75-point tightening also was the largest one-time rate increase under the chairmanship of Alan Greenspan.
The long bond's performance matters to the Fed because it provides information about inflation expectations and policy credibility -- as outlined by Greenspan in February 1994.

"The test of successful monetary policy in such a business-cycle phase is our ability to limit the upward movement of long-term rates from what it would otherwise have been with less effective policy," Greenspan told Congress.
Fed records show the relevant magnitude of the initial move in the preemptive tightening cycle was already debated in December of 1993.
Then Governor Wayne Angell dissented in favor of an immediate move, along with Governor Lawrence Lindsey. However, only Angell favored a bold 50-basis-point move at the time.

One source said the bond yield's 1994 performance, in retrospect, showed small 25-point moves were more unsettling to the market than bolder actions because they were unlikely to require another rate adjustment in the near future.
"The issue with moving toward price stability is finding a more effective way to convey our intention," the source said.

Former Fed Vice Chairman Alan Blinder said there are two big questions for monetary policy: (1) deciding whether current inflationary pressures require immediate action, and (2) determining how to achieve long-term price stability.

"We are close enough to price stability that the Fed has to think seriously about where its long-term goal is and how rapidly does it need to approach that goal," Blinder said. "The other question is more short-term, judging the extent of the slowdowm and whether we should expect an uptick in inflation."
Blinder, however, stressed that the answer to either question is not fundamentally different.

"What policy actions of today do to inflation three years from today is more or less the same as what they do to inflation 10 years from today because there is a lot of inertia in inflation," Blinder said.
Former Fed Staff Director Stephen Axilrod acknowledged it is difficult for the central bank to control how the Treasury market reacts to Fed decisions.

"This may be a problem but it's hard to put that in real operational terms," Axilrod, an advisor to consulting firm MFR Inc, said. "The market may or may not expect you to do more. If you start tightening, there are people with long positions who will have to get out."
Compounding the market's problem in correctly reading the Fed's intentions is the fact the central bank has avoided adopting any monetary policy target.
New York Fed President William McDonough, in a March 21 address, suggested targeting the Consumer Price Index (CPI).

McDonough, acknowledging the possibility of a bias in the CPI, proposed targeting a 0.5- to 2.0-percent range. He reiterated the benefits of targeting an inflation gauge last week, refining the notion to targeting core CPI. The core rate excludes volatile food and energy items.
McDonough's views are shared, to a large extent, by other Fed presidents.

Cleveland's Jerry Jordan pioneered the notion in 1992; San Francisco's Robert Parry endorsed McDonough's CPI range; St. Louis's Thomas Melzer stated the need to "clearly state our objective ... and accept accountability," and Minneapolis's Gary Stern said setting an inflation range would be more realistic than setting a specific target.
